rv.q: Jonathan Munby’s production relishes every detail. Though perhaps a touch too spry, Goodman, 76, nevertheless steals the first half as the endearing interloper, by turns calculating, stoical, impatient, and roguishly eccentric
Goodman, a spry and springy 76, gives little sense of decrepitude but superbly captures Solomon’s spirit.
As with many of Miller’s better-known plays, it’s implacable: the past piles into the present and the action cannot stop until all the truths are out.
You end up wondering why this angry, plaintive and deeply psychological play is not more often revived.
Miller's script crackles with sharp, uncomfortable insights and unspoken, long-nurtured grievances.
Even a lesser Miller is greater than most.
The results are astounding, this adaptation is as good as the play can be.
The Price offers no easy answers, just a finely balanced reckoning.

From sedate beginnings, Miller builds the simmering familial scene to an emotional crescendo which is frequently and humorously broken by the re-emergence from the bedroom, of the elderly and meddling Solomon who has his eyes on the prize and won’t be deterred.
The tension in this second act makes it more of a thrill to witness than the more humorous Act I.
The play is an interesting curio from Miller’s oeuvre, but this production needs to make a stronger case for revisiting it.

All the actor’s do Miller’s script proud, with some allowed to forge ahead with their character’s ambitions, such as Walter who achieves his career goals, and Gregory Solomon, a man filled with chutzpah and still excited by a furniture deal in his ninth decade of life

cn.t: Miller's underrated 1967 drama earns strong reviews for its superbly acted family tensions and sharp psychological insights, with Henry Goodman's scene-stealing furniture dealer winning particular praise in this well-crafted revival.
